\begin{example}\label{ex:categories}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The \emph{concrete} categories: $\mathbf{Set}$ (sets and maps), $\mathbf{Grp}$ (groups and homomorphisms), $\mathbf{Ab}$ (abelian groups), $\mathbf{Ring}$ (rings with $1$ and
homomorphisms preserving $1$), $\mathbf{CRing}$ (commutative rings), $R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}$ (modules over a ring $R$ and $R$-linear maps), $\mathbf{Vect}_K$ (vector spaces over a field $K$),
$\mathbf{Top}$ (topological spaces and continuous maps), $\mathbf{Top}_*$ (spaces with a base point and maps preserving it). Composition is composition of maps.
\item A \emph{poset} $(P,\le)$ is a category with one morphism $x\to y$ when $x\le y$ and none otherwise; reflexivity gives the identities and transitivity the composition.
\item A \emph{monoid} $M$ is a category with one object $\bullet$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(\bullet,\bullet)=M$, composition being the product of $M$. A group is a one-object category in which every
morphism has an inverse.
\item $\mathbf{Mat}_K$ has the natural numbers as objects, the $m\times n$ matrices as morphisms $n\to m$, and the product of matrices as composition. Nothing in it is a set with
structure: a morphism is not a map between anything.
\item The \emph{opposite} category $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the objects of $\mathcal C$, $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}}(A,B)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(B,A)$, and composition reversed.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:functors}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \emph{Forgetful functors} $U\colon\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathbf{Ring}\to\mathbf{Ab}$, $\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Set}$, which forget part of the structure.
\item \emph{Abelianisation} $\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Ab}$, $G\mapsto G^{\mathrm{ab}}=G/G'$, where $G'$ is the subgroup generated by the commutators $aba^{-1}b^{-1}$ (Volume~3, Exercise~2.4). A homomorphism $f\colon G\to H$ maps commutators to commutators, hence $G'$ into $H'$, and induces $f^{\mathrm{ab}}\colon gG'\mapsto f(g)H'$.
\item The units $R\mapsto R^\times$ and $R\mapsto\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ are functors $\mathbf{CRing}\to\mathbf{Grp}$: a ring homomorphism, applied to each entry, maps invertible matrices to invertible
matrices.
\item The fundamental group $\pi_1\colon\mathbf{Top}_*\to\mathbf{Grp}$ (Volume~9, Chapter~5), and the homology groups $H_n\colon\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Ab}$ (Volume~9, Chapter~6). That $H_n(g\circ f)=H_n(g)\circ H_n(f)$
was proved there; it is exactly the statement that $H_n$ is a functor.
\item Duality $V\mapsto V^*=\operatorname{Hom}(V,K)$, $f\mapsto f^*=(\varphi\mapsto\varphi\circ f)$, is a contravariant functor $\mathbf{Vect}_K\to\mathbf{Vect}_K$: $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$.
\item For an object $A$ of any category, the functor $h^A=\operatorname{Hom}(A,-)$ from $\mathcal C$ to $\mathbf{Set}$ sends $B$ to $\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)$ and $g\colon B\to C$ to $g\circ-$. Likewise
the contravariant functor $h_A=\operatorname{Hom}(-,A)$ sends $g\colon B\to C$ to the map $-\circ g$ from $\operatorname{Hom}(C,A)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}(B,A)$.
\item A functor between two posets is an order-preserving map; a functor between two groups, seen as one-object categories, is a homomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:products}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item In $\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathbf{Grp}$, $\mathbf{Ring}$ and $R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}$ the product is the cartesian product with componentwise operations: $h(x)=(f(x),g(x))$ is the only possibility, and it is a
morphism.
\item In $\mathbf{Top}$ the product is $A\times B$ with the product topology, and the universal property explains the definition of that topology: it is the coarsest one making both projections
continuous, which is exactly what is needed for every $(f,g)$ with $f$, $g$ continuous to be continuous.
\item In a poset, $x\times y$ is the greatest lower bound $\inf(x,y)$, and $x\sqcup y$ the least upper bound, when they exist. In the poset of positive integers ordered by divisibility, they are the
$\gcd$ and the $\operatorname{lcm}$.
\item In $\mathbf{Set}$ the coproduct is the disjoint union. In $R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}$ it is the direct sum $A\oplus B$ with $i_A(a)=(a,0)$, $i_B(b)=(0,b)$ and $h(a,b)=f(a)+g(b)$: the same object as the product,
a coincidence special to additive categories. In $\mathbf{Grp}$ the formula $h(a,b)=f(a)g(b)$ is not a homomorphism unless the images commute, and the coproduct is the free product $A*B$ of Volume~9,
Proposition~5.17, whose universal property is exactly the one required.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{example}[the natural operations on groups]\label{ex:natops}
Which operations $G\to G$, $g\mapsto w_G(g)$, can be defined on every group, compatibly with all homomorphisms, that is, with $f(w_G(g))=w_H(f(g))$ for every $f\colon G\to H$? Such a family is exactly a natural
transformation $U\Rightarrow U$, where $U\colon\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is the forgetful functor. Now $U$ is representable: $U\cong h^{\Z}$, since a homomorphism $f\colon\Z\to G$ is the same as the element $f(1)$. By Yoneda,
\[\operatorname{Nat}(U,U)\cong\operatorname{Nat}(h^{\Z},U)\cong U(\Z)=\Z.\]
The transformation attached to $n\in\Z$ sends $g=f(1)$ to $f(n)=g^n$. So the only operations on one element that make sense in every group are the powers $g\mapsto g^n$: there is no other formula, however
clever. Exercise~\ref{ex:words} does the same for operations on two elements.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:adjunctions}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \emph{Free and forgetful.} The free module functor $S\mapsto R^{(S)}$ is left adjoint to the forgetful functor $U\colon R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}\to\mathbf{Set}$: linear maps $R^{(S)}\to M$ correspond to maps $S\to U(M)$, by restriction to the
basis. The same holds for the free group on a set (Volume~9, Chapter~5) and the polynomial ring $\Z[X_s:s\in S]$, free commutative ring on $S$.
\item \emph{Abelianisation.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:abuniv}, $G\mapsto G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ is left adjoint to the inclusion $\mathbf{Ab}\to\mathbf{Grp}$: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Ab}}(G^{\mathrm{ab}},A)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(G,A)$ by $\bar f\mapsto\bar f\circ\pi_G$.
\item \emph{Currying.} In $\mathbf{Set}$, for a fixed set $B$, maps $A\times B\to C$ correspond to maps $A\to C^B$ (the set of maps $B\to C$): $h\mapsto(a\mapsto h(a,-))$. So $-\times B\dashv(-)^B$. Programmers call this
\emph{currying}, after Haskell Curry.
\item \emph{Topologies.} The discrete topology $\mathbf{Set}\to\mathbf{Top}$ is left adjoint to the forgetful functor (every map out of a discrete space is continuous), and the indiscrete topology is right adjoint to it (every
map into an indiscrete space is continuous).
\item \emph{Galois connections.} Between posets, an adjunction $F\dashv G$ means $F(x)\le y\iff x\le G(y)$. For a finite Galois extension $L/K$ with group $\Gamma$, the maps $H\mapsto L^H$ from subgroups of $\Gamma$ to
intermediate fields, and $E\mapsto\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)$, both reverse inclusions, and $E\subseteq L^H\iff H\subseteq\operatorname{Gal}(L/E)$: an adjunction between the poset of subgroups and the opposite of the poset of
intermediate fields. The general notion is named after this example; the fundamental theorem of Galois theory (Volume~3, Chapter~10) says that here the adjunction is an equivalence.
\end{enumerate}
\end{example}

\begin{definition}\label{linear:def:kronecker}
The \emph{Kronecker product} of $A\in M_{m,n}(\C)$ and $B\in M_{p,q}(\C)$ is the $mp\times nq$ block matrix
\[
A\otimes B=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}B&\cdots&a_{1n}B\\\vdots&&\vdots\\a_{m1}B&\cdots&a_{mn}B\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For vectors this is $(u\otimes v)_{(i,k)}=u_iv_k$, the coordinates being ordered lexicographically.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}[the rank depends on the field]\label{linear:exa:rotation}
Let $T$ have slices $A=I$ and $B=J=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, the rotation by a quarter turn. Then
$A^{-1}B=J$ has eigenvalues $\pm i$: it is diagonalisable over $\C$ but not over $\R$. So $R_\C(T)=2$ but $R_\R(T)\ge3$. In fact
$R_\R(T)=3$, as the decomposition
\[
T=(1,1)\otimes(0,1)\otimes(1,0)+(-1,1)\otimes(1,0)\otimes(0,1)+(1,0)\otimes(1,-1)\otimes(1,1)
\]
shows (check the two slices). The rank of a real tensor can drop when complex numbers are allowed, which never happens for
matrices. The same tensor appears in disguise in Exercise~\ref{linear:ex:complexmult}: it is the multiplication of complex numbers.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[rank is not semicontinuous]\label{linear:exa:wtensor}
The tensor
\[
W=e_1\otimes e_1\otimes e_2+e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_1+e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_1
\]
(Figure~\ref{linear:fig:wtensor}; physicists call it the W~state of three qubits) has slices $A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0
\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, and $A^{-1}B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&0
\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ is nilpotent and non-zero, hence not diagonalisable over any field. So $R(W)=3$. But for $\varepsilon\ne0$,
\[
W_\varepsilon=\frac1\varepsilon\Bigl((e_1+\varepsilon e_2)^{\otimes3}-e_1^{\otimes3}\Bigr)=W+\varepsilon\,(e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_2+
e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_2+e_2\otimes e_2\otimes e_1)+\varepsilon^2e_2^{\otimes3}
\]
has rank at most $2$, and $W_\varepsilon\to W$. A limit of tensors of rank $2$ has rank $3$.
\end{example}

\begin{definition}\label{linear:def:mmtensor}
The \emph{matrix multiplication tensor} $\langle n,m,p\rangle$ is the tensor in $K^{nm}\otimes K^{mp}\otimes K^{pn}$ given by
\[
\langle n,m,p\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^pe_{ij}\otimes e_{jk}\otimes e_{ki},
\]
where $e_{ij}$ denotes the matrix unit. As a trilinear form it is $(A,B,C)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(ABC)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Strassen, 1969]\label{linear:thm:strassen}
$R(\langle2,2,2\rangle)\le7$. Explicitly, for $2\times2$ matrices $A,B$ (whose entries may lie in any ring, commutative or not),
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_1&=(a_{11}+a_{22})(b_{11}+b_{22}),&M_5&=(a_{11}+a_{12})b_{22},\\
M_2&=(a_{21}+a_{22})b_{11},&M_6&=(a_{21}-a_{11})(b_{11}+b_{12}),\\
M_3&=a_{11}(b_{12}-b_{22}),&M_7&=(a_{12}-a_{22})(b_{21}+b_{22}),\\
M_4&=a_{22}(b_{21}-b_{11}),
\end{aligned}
\]
and then
\[
AB=\begin{pmatrix}M_1+M_4-M_5+M_7&M_3+M_5\\M_2+M_4&M_1-M_2+M_3+M_6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Schmidt decomposition]\label{linear:thm:schmidt}
Every $\psi\in\C^m\otimes\C^n$ can be written
\[
\psi=\sum_{s=1}^r\sigma_s\,a_s\otimes b_s,
\]
with $(a_s)$ orthonormal in $\C^m$, $(b_s)$ orthonormal in $\C^n$, and $\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_r>0$. The numbers $\sigma_s$ are the
singular values of the coefficient matrix $\Psi=(\psi_{ij})$, and $r=\operatorname{rank}\Psi$. In particular, $\psi$ is a product
state if and only if $\operatorname{rank}\Psi=1$, and $\sum_s\sigma_s^2=\|\psi\|^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}\label{def:fractional}
A \emph{fractional ideal} of $R$ is a non-zero $R$-submodule $I\subseteq K$ such that $dI\subseteq R$ for some non-zero $d\in R$. The product $IJ$ is the submodule generated by the products $xy$, $x\in I$, $y\in J$,
and
\[
(R:I)=\{x\in K: xI\subseteq R\}.
\]
$I$ is \emph{invertible} if $IJ=R$ for some fractional ideal $J$.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}\label{ex:sixtwice}
In $R=\Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the two factorisations $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ of the number $6$ come from one factorisation of the ideal $6R$. With
$\mathfrak p=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$, $\mathfrak q=(3,1+\sqrt{-5})$ and $\bar{\mathfrak q}=(3,1-\sqrt{-5})$, one has (Exercise~\ref{ex:zsqrt5})
\[
2R=\mathfrak p^2,\quad 3R=\mathfrak q\bar{\mathfrak q},\quad (1+\sqrt{-5})=\mathfrak p\mathfrak q,\quad(1-\sqrt{-5})=\mathfrak p\bar{\mathfrak q},
\]
so both factorisations of $6$ regroup the same four prime ideals $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q,\bar{\mathfrak q}$. None of these primes is principal.

The ring $R$ is Dedekind because it is the integral closure of $\Z$ in $L=\Q(\sqrt{-5})$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:intclosure} applies. To see that the
integral closure is no larger, let $y=a+b\sqrt{-5}$ with $a,b\in\Q$ be integral over $\Z$. The matrix of multiplication by $y$ in the basis
$1,\sqrt{-5}$ has trace $2a$ and determinant $a^2+5b^2$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:trace} its characteristic polynomial has integer coefficients. So
$A=2a$ and $4(a^2+5b^2)=A^2+5B^2$, with $B=2b$, are integers. Then $5B^2$ is an integer; a denominator of $B$ would appear squared in $5B^2$, so
$B\in\Z$. Finally $A^2+5B^2\equiv A^2+B^2\equiv0\pmod 4$, and since squares are $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$, both $A$ and $B$ are even: $a,b\in\Z$.
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:classseq}
The sequence of abelian groups
\[
1\longrightarrow R^\times\longrightarrow K^\times\xrightarrow{\ x\,\mapsto\, xR\ }\mathcal I(R)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Cl}(R)\longrightarrow1
\]
is exact, and $R$ is a principal ideal domain if and only if $\operatorname{Cl}(R)=1$, if and only if $R$ is a unique factorisation domain.
\end{proposition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:resolution}
A \emph{projective resolution} of a module $M$ is an exact sequence
\[
\cdots\to P_2\xrightarrow{d_2}P_1\xrightarrow{d_1}P_0\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}M\to0
\]
with all $P_n$ projective. We write $P_\bullet\to M$, and $P_\bullet$ for the complex $\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to0$, whose homology is $M$ in degree $0$ and $0$ elsewhere.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}\label{def:torext}
Let $P_\bullet\to M$ be a projective resolution and $N$ a module. Then
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_n^R(M,N)=H_n(P_\bullet\otimes N),\qquad\operatorname{Ext}^n_R(M,N)=H^n\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(P_\bullet,N)\bigr),
\]
the homology of the complex $\cdots\to P_1\otimes N\to P_0\otimes N\to0$ and the cohomology of $0\to\operatorname{Hom}(P_0,N)\to\operatorname{Hom}(P_1,N)\to\cdots$.
\end{definition}

\begin{example}\label{ex:torextz}
Over $\Z$, use $0\to\Z\xrightarrow n\Z\to\Z/n\to0$. Tensoring with $N$ gives $N\xrightarrow nN$, and applying $\operatorname{Hom}(-,N)$ gives $N\xrightarrow nN$ again (as $\operatorname{Hom}(\Z,N)=N$). Hence
\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1(\Z/n,N)\cong N[n]=\{x\in N:nx=0\},\qquad\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/n,N)\cong N/nN,
\]
and both vanish in degrees $\ge2$. In particular $\operatorname{Tor}_1(\Z/m,\Z/n)\cong\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/m,\Z/n)\cong\Z/d$ with $d=\gcd(m,n)$, and $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Z/n,\Z)\cong\Z/n$. The group
$\operatorname{Tor}_1(\Z/n,N)$ is the $n$-torsion of $N$, which explains the name: Tor detects torsion.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:rp2uct}
The cell structure of Figure~\ref{fig:surfaces} gives for $\R P^2$ the complex $\Z\xrightarrow{2}\Z\xrightarrow{0}\Z$ (degrees $2,1,0$), so $H_0=\Z$, $H_1=\Z/2$, $H_2=0$. With $A=\Z/2$ the theorem predicts
\[
H_2(\R P^2;\Z/2)\cong H_2\otimes\Z/2\oplus\operatorname{Tor}_1(H_1,\Z/2)=0\oplus\Z/2,
\]
and directly, $\Z/2\xrightarrow{0}\Z/2\xrightarrow{0}\Z/2$ has $H_2=\Z/2$. For cohomology with integer coefficients, $H^2(\R P^2;\Z)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(H_2,\Z)\oplus\operatorname{Ext}^1(H_1,\Z)=\Z/2$, although $H_2=0$:
in cohomology the torsion moves up one degree.
\end{example}

\begin{example}\label{ex:pythagoras}
For $\Q(i)/\Q$, $\sigma$ is complex conjugation and $N(a+bi)=a^2+b^2$. A rational point $(a,b)$ on the unit circle is an element of norm $1$, so $a+bi=\beta/\bar\beta$ with $\beta\in\Q(i)^\times$, and after clearing denominators
$\beta=m+ni$ with $m,n\in\Z$. Then
\[
a+bi=\frac{m+ni}{m-ni}=\frac{(m+ni)^2}{m^2+n^2}=\frac{m^2-n^2}{m^2+n^2}+\frac{2mn}{m^2+n^2}\,i.
\]
This is the classical parametrisation of Pythagorean triples $(m^2-n^2,2mn,m^2+n^2)$ (Volume~2, Chapter~8, Theorem~8.1), now seen as the vanishing of a cohomology group (Figure~\ref{fig:rationalcircle}).
\end{example}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:wedderburnCG}
Let $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_r$ be the irreducible representations of $G$, of dimensions $d_1,\dots,d_r$. The map
\[
\C[G]\to\prod_{i=1}^r\operatorname{End}(V_i)\cong\prod_{i=1}^rM_{d_i}(\C),\qquad a\mapsto\bigl(\rho_1(a),\dots,\rho_r(a)\bigr),
\]
is an isomorphism of algebras. The centre of $\C[G]$, spanned by the class sums $\sum_{g\in C}g$, corresponds to the scalar matrices, and the element
\[
e_i=\frac{d_i}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi_i(g^{-1})\,g
\]
is the central idempotent that is the identity on $V_i$ and $0$ on $V_j$ for $j\ne i$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}\label{def:induced}
Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ and $W$ a representation of $H$. The \emph{induced representation} is
\[
\operatorname{Ind}_H^GW=\{f\colon G\to W:\ f(hx)=h\cdot f(x)\text{ for all }h\in H,\ x\in G\},
\]
with $G$ acting by right translation, $(g\cdot f)(x)=f(xg)$. For a representation $V$ of $G$, $\operatorname{Res}_HV$ is $V$ viewed as a representation of $H$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Frobenius reciprocity, 1898]\label{thm:frobrecip}
For representations $V$ of $G$ and $W$ of $H$, the map $T\mapsto\mathrm{ev}_1\circ T$, where $\mathrm{ev}_1(f)=f(1)$, is an isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_G\bigl(V,\operatorname{Ind}_H^GW\bigr)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H\bigl(\operatorname{Res}_HV,W\bigr).
\]
So induction is right adjoint to restriction (Chapter~1), and $\langle\chi_V,\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\psi\rangle_G=\langle\operatorname{Res}_H\chi_V,\psi\rangle_H$ for the characters.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}\label{def:tabloid}
Two tableaux $T,T'$ of shape $\lambda$ are \emph{row equivalent} if $T'=\pi T$ for some $\pi\in R_T$, that is, if they have the same rows as sets. The class $\{T\}$ is a \emph{tabloid}. The permutation module $M^\lambda$ is the
vector space with basis the tabloids of shape $\lambda$, with $\sigma\{T\}=\{\sigma T\}$. For a tableau $T$, let
\[
\kappa_T=\sum_{\pi\in C_T}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\,\pi\in\C[\mathfrak S_n],\qquad e_T=\kappa_T\{T\}\in M^\lambda.
\]
The element $e_T$ is a \emph{polytabloid}, and the \emph{Specht module} $S^\lambda$ is the subspace of $M^\lambda$ spanned by all polytabloids.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Robinson--Schensted correspondence]\label{thm:rs}
For $\sigma\in\mathfrak S_n$, let $P(\sigma)=(\cdots((\emptyset\leftarrow\sigma(1))\leftarrow\sigma(2))\cdots)\leftarrow\sigma(n)$, and let $Q(\sigma)$ be the tableau of the same shape whose cell added at step $k$ holds $k$. Then
$\sigma\mapsto(P(\sigma),Q(\sigma))$ is a bijection from $\mathfrak S_n$ to the set of pairs of standard tableaux of the same shape. Consequently
\[
\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2=n!,
\]
and $\dim S^\lambda=f^\lambda$: the standard polytabloids form a basis of $S^\lambda$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Peter--Weyl, 1927]\label{thm:peterweyl}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $\mathcal R(G)$ is dense in $C(G)$ for the uniform norm.
\item The functions $\sqrt{d_\rho}\,\rho_{ij}$, for $\rho\in\widehat G$ and $1\le i,j\le d_\rho$, form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(G,\mu)$. So every $f\in L^2$ is the $L^2$-convergent sum of its \emph{Fourier series}
\[
f=\sum_{\rho\in\widehat G}d_\rho\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\hat f(\rho)\rho\bigr),\qquad\hat f(\rho)=\int_Gf(g)\rho(g)^*\dd\mu(g),
\]
with the Plancherel identity
\[
\int_G|f|^2\dd\mu=\sum_\rho d_\rho\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\hat f(\rho)\hat f(\rho)^*\bigr).
\]
\item The characters $\chi_\rho$, $\rho\in\widehat G$, form an orthonormal basis of the closed subspace of $L^2(G,\mu)$ of class functions, those with $f(hgh^{-1})=f(g)$ for all $h$ and almost every $g$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:alternants}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item $s_\lambda$ is a symmetric Laurent polynomial with integer coefficients; its largest monomial in the lexicographic order is $t^\lambda$, with coefficient $1$.
\item Every antisymmetric Laurent polynomial is a unique finite combination $\sum_\mu c_\mu a_\mu$ over strictly decreasing $\mu$, with $c_\mu$ its coefficient of $t^\mu$.
\item For strictly decreasing $\mu,\nu$,
\[
\frac1{n!}\int_T a_\mu\overline{a_\nu}\,\frac{\dd\theta}{(2\pi)^n}=\delta_{\mu\nu},
\]
where $t_j=e^{i\theta_j}$ and $\dd\theta=\dd\theta_1\cdots\dd\theta_n$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Diaconis--Shahshahani 1994, Rains 1998]\label{thm:traces}
For every $a\ge0$, $(\operatorname{tr}U)^a=\sum_{\lambda\vdash a,\ \ell(\lambda)\le n}f^\lambda\chi_{V_\lambda}(U)$, and
\[
\mathbb E\bigl|\operatorname{tr}U\bigr|^{2a}=\#\bigl\{\sigma\in\mathfrak S_a:\ \text{the longest increasing subsequence of $\sigma$ has length}\le n\bigr\}.
\]
In particular $\mathbb E|\operatorname{tr}U|^{2a}=a!$ whenever $a\le n$.
\end{theorem}
